case.description: Create a reusable joint between two square rods in a tabletop pointer frame. The joint must let the operator exchange either rod while restoring the pointer's marked position without altering the rods.
case.valued_outcome: After five exchanges of each rod, the pointer returns within a 2 mm target circle and remains there during a supplied 10 N lateral load for ten seconds; each exchange takes less than forty seconds.
hard_constraints: No drilling, adhesive or permanent marks on either rod.
Joint envelope must fit inside a 90 mm cube.
Only hand-operated assembly and adjustment are permitted.
No component may fall free during an exchange.
resources: Two 400 mm square rods, measured sides 19 mm and 20 mm, plus one pointer and marked base.
Six plywood pieces each 80 by 40 by 6 mm, eight M5 bolts with nuts, four washers, two 150 mm elastic loops and 0.5 m of cord.
Hand drill for plywood only, saw, file, screwdriver and ruler.
One hundred minutes for fabrication and twenty minutes for testing.
observations: The current loose joint lets the pointer move 7 mm under the load.
Rod ends are square within the supplied 1 mm measurement resolution.
Awkward observation: the visually tighter rod fit returned 3 mm farther from the target after exchange than the looser fit in two supplied trials.

openings.claim: The supplied clamp function alone may restrain this joint sufficiently after manual pointer repositioning. This is an ordinary clamp hypothesis, not a measured improvement.
openings.delta: Replace reliance on visually tight clearance with adjustable closing force carried by plywood jaws and M5 bolts pressing both rods against contact faces. Reposition the pointer against its existing base target before tightening; add no insertion stop. Keep jaws attached with elastic loops and tether bolts, nuts and washers with cord, with all joint components inside 90 mm.
openings.prediction: Compared with the nearest rival, the same jaws set to contact-only pressure, hand-tightened jaws should show less target departure under 10 N. After each exchange and target-guided adjustment, the candidate should remain within the 2 mm circle for ten seconds, including the 18 mm replacement, with exchanges under forty seconds. Failure to return accurately despite reduced load movement defeats the complete outcome claim.
openings.probe: Within 100 fabrication minutes, attempt one captive jaw body using only supplied materials and hand tools. Before testing, verify envelope, retained hardware and adjustable travel across 18–20 mm. Compare contact-only and hand-tightened settings, each with five exchanges of each original rod followed by two exchanges using the 18 mm replacement. Apply four ten-second 10 N load trials per setting after exchanges 2, 5, 10 and 12; log exchange times and pointer positions before and during loading. First budget the swaps, eight loads and setting changes against twenty minutes. If fabrication, captivity, timing or readable target displacement cannot be achieved, report feasibility unresolved; the caps alone establish no informative test. This is a probe, not deployment.
assumptions: Six plywood pieces and eight bolts can form connected jaws with sufficient travel, stiffness and captive retention inside the envelope; a workable layout is unproven.
Existing target permits hand repositioning within forty seconds without marking rods.
Hand tightening force is uncontrolled; slipping, plywood deformation, tether interference or indistinguishable closing pressures can defeat or confound the comparison.

artifact.assessment: One opening: adjustable clamping only. Accurate return and load restraint remain separate required observations; the supplied tighter-fit anomaly supports testing rather than predicting success.

openings.claim: Couple the known insertion stop A to clamp B through contact-gated tightening: restraint begins only after the rod reaches its stop. This might prevent the tighter-fit return error without altering either rod.
openings.delta: Change the assembly dependency from independent tightening to seat-then-tighten. Propose two adjustable plywood rod saddles with fixed end stops, hand-tightened M5 restraint, and cord/elastic retention of every loosened component. Geometry within 90 mm and retention remain fabrication questions.
openings.prediction: Nearest rival: ordinary additive benefit from a stop plus tighter restraint. Coupling predicts lower pointer displacement for intact A×B than for identical parents with tightening performed before stop contact. For lateral displacement d, test whether 7−dAB exceeds (7−dA)+(7−dB), and whether breaking the sequence removes that excess. These are proposed comparisons, not measured synergy; exchange repeatability could disagree.
openings.probe: Use supplied 7 mm loose-joint displacement as baseline. In the intact configuration, compare A alone with restraint released, B alone with stop contact bypassed, and intact A×B, allocating four load trials across these modes. In the second configuration retain every parent component but break only the seating-to-tightening interface; allocate four load trials. Run twelve exchanges per configuration: five of each original rod, then two replacing the 19 mm rod with 18 mm. Log return error, ten-second 10 N displacement, exchange time, initial setup and readjustment burden. Parent-only modes provide load screening, not full exchange validation. If release modes count as extra configurations, this comparison exceeds the cap and cannot proceed as specified.
assumptions: Six plywood pieces and supplied hardware can form two retained saddles within the envelope; unverified.
Square end contacts remain reproducible across supplied size variation; unverified.
Defeat: no interaction beyond additive benefit, broken interface performs equally, any return exceeds 2 mm, load escape, exchange reaches forty seconds, or fabrication/testing exceeds 100/20 minutes.
Capacity to complete screening plus exchanges within twenty minutes is unknown; the stop cap alone establishes no informative feasible test.

openings.claim: Separate locating from gripping: each rod seats against two fixed adjacent faces and an end stop; an opposing adjustable plywood jaw presses it into those datums. Clearance elsewhere permits exchange without requiring a tight surrounding fit.
openings.delta: Change the positioning dependency from enclosing fit to fixed datum contacts and seat-before-clamp action. Drill plywood only; preserve the frame rod relationship within a measured 90 mm envelope.

The datum mechanism instead predicts that correctly seated clearance can return closer after exchange while resisting load. Distinguishing observations are target displacement before loading, displacement during loading, and exchange time; the supplied two trials establish neither explanation.

Hand tools can produce stable datum contacts and sufficient jaw stiffness; this is unmeasured.
Defeat: datum rocking, plywood bending, slip under load, or 18 mm travel exhaustion can invalidate the mechanism even with good unloaded return.

openings.claim: Preserve insertion stops and adjustable elastic clamps, but disconnect their simultaneous load-bearing interface: swing each stop clear only after its rod is clamped. The clamp alone then maintains the registered position.
openings.delta: Tentatively use four trimmed plywood pieces as two orthogonal datum seats and the remaining two as captive pivoting stop leaves. Bolts join seats, pivot leaves and anchor adjustable elastic loops; cord retains loose hardware. Keep the entire joint within 90 mm. Each stop still supplies a fixed insertion contact while closed. After clamping, retract both leaves without compensating rod adjustments. Comparator uses the same assembly with leaves remaining engaged.
openings.prediction: If stop contact competing with clamp seating causes exchange error, retracted leaves should reduce return displacement, especially on the 18 mm substitution, without increased loaded displacement. Nearest rival: clamp friction/compliance or operator seating causes the error; retracting stops then provides no repeatability advantage or worsens drift. These are speculative mechanisms, not explanations established by the two supplied trials.

Alternate configuration blocks, restore the marked setup before each block, and record elapsed exchange time and pointer return displacement. Give each configuration four ten-second 10 N load trials spanning both rod sizes; record displacement during loading. Include retraction time in exchanges. Do not reseat after retraction. Twelve exchanges do not establish the full original-rod endurance outcome under every load.

Elastic loops provide adjustable closing force against datums without rod modification; capacity is unknown.
Stop retraction clears rods without disturbing their clamped positions.
Defeat: return advantage absent, any target/load/time failure, hardware escape, envelope excess, or fabrication/testing budget exceeded. All constraints remain binding.

openings.claim: Make return position depend on fixed face datums and insertion stops, with clamping applied after seating. The nearest rival is that tighter enclosure alone improves return accuracy; the awkward trials do not establish either explanation.
openings.delta: Within the 90 mm joint envelope, cut plywood into two connected corner saddles with captured end-stop offcuts and captive clamp yokes. Allocate four bolts to saddle/carrier/stop fastening and four to the yokes. Recess nuts and retain yokes and fasteners with the supplied cord/loops. Hand-open each yoke without dismantling the carrier, seat the rod against two faces and its stop, then tighten. Preserve the frame angle established at the marked pointer position.
openings.prediction: If inconsistent seating explains the tight-fit penalty, seating before clamping should produce fewer target misses than inserting under partial clamp pressure, despite identical final tightening. The 18 mm substitution should still reach the same datums after adjustment. Persistent misses despite verified seating, or load drift above the target boundary, defeat the proposed repeatability or restraint mechanism.
openings.probe: First check bolt reach, captive retention, saddle rigidity and full opening within the envelope using the available hardware. Fabricate within 100 minutes only if those checks succeed. Compare two procedural configurations on the same joint: seat-then-clamp and insert-under-partial-clamp. Each gets five exchanges of each original rod, then two exchanges replacing the 19 mm rod with 18 mm. Log elapsed exchange time and target return; apply 10 N for ten seconds initially and after exchanges 9, 10 and 12. Record seating gaps and loaded pointer movement. Twenty minutes leaves only 160 seconds for logging/reset if exchanges approach forty seconds; abandon the comparison as inconclusive if overhead cannot fit.
assumptions: Unspecified bolt lengths permit the proposed plywood stack and yokes.
Six pieces provide adequate captured stop material and stiffness; cord/loops suffice for retention.
Hand tightening supplies sufficient restraint without damaging or marking rods.
Actual fabrication and measurement overhead fit the supplied time budgets.

artifact.assessment: A bounded prototype probe, with capacity and construction unresolved. No supplied observation establishes success under load, exchange timing, retention or replacement-rod tolerance; deployment requires those checks to pass.

openings.claim: Use fixed plywood end stops to make each rod insertion terminate at a repeatable contact plane. This tests the first known parent function alone; it does not establish loaded pointer stability.
openings.delta: Replace operator-selected insertion depth with rod-end contact against captive end blocks in loose crossed plywood channels. Make clearance keepers and hardware captive with the supplied cord or elastic loops, without closing pressure or rod modification. Keep the complete assembly inside 90 mm in every dimension. The nearest rival uses identical channels and captive stops disengaged, with depth set by ruler.
openings.prediction: If insertion-depth variation contributes materially to return error, active stops should reduce unloaded pointer displacement after exchanges compared with ruler-set depth. If clearance, seating angle or rod-size change dominates, depth contact may repeat while pointer error remains or increases. The tighter-fit observation prevents assuming tighter channels improve return.
openings.probe: Within the fabrication allowance, make one fixture with two captive stop positions: active and disengaged. Use only supplied plywood, hardware, tethers and tools; no clamping preload. Within twenty testing minutes, run twelve exchanges per configuration: first five of each original rod, then two exchanges using the 18 mm replacement. Log exchange times and target displacement; apply four ten-second 10 N lateral trials per configuration after exchanges 2, 6, 10 and 12. Compare return and loaded displacement using the target card, ruler and scale. Check captivity and envelope before exchange testing. Fabrication or timing failure leaves the comparison unresolved.
assumptions: Available offcuts, eight bolts and tethers suffice for fixed channels, stops and captive clearance keepers within one hundred fabrication minutes; this is unverified.
Stop contact is observable and comparable across configurations without altering rods.

Defeat conditions include no return improvement, missed 2 mm target, movement during load, any exchange taking forty seconds or more, and failure with the 18 mm rod. Passive channel clearance may prevent meeting the valued outcome.

artifact.assessment: A bounded probe of end-contact positioning, with the full return, load, time, captivity and replacement requirements retained. No deployment or reliable performance is claimed. A stop alone does not demonstrate sufficient lateral or angular restraint.
